title: Sold a Story Season 2: Hopes, Dreams, and Questions
author: Kata Solow
summary: Writing after the first two episodes of Season 2 of the Sold a Story podcast, which turns to Direct Instruction, the author sets out what she hopes the series will and will not do. She credits Zig Engelmann's work with lessons teachers can use, including relentless student response, frequent checks for understanding, examples and non-examples, short explanations and constant review. She also values his mantra that when a student does not understand, the teaching is probably at fault, and his belief that young children can do hard things. She hopes Emily Hanford will complicate the story, citing a Downs and Hiebert study in which a challenging-text fluency routine matched a DI program on fluency and beat it on accuracy. She closes with open questions about how DI programs develop robust comprehension and where student interpretation fits.
points: Direct Instruction offers transferable classroom habits, such as constant student response, checks for understanding, short explanations and cumulative review, that teachers can adopt without adopting a whole program.
Engelmann’s premise that failure to learn points to the teaching rather than the student is presented as a mindset that makes teachers more persistent and more in control of their work.

A third-grade intervention study found that reading above-grade-level text with scaffolded fluency routines produced greater accuracy gains than a controlled-text DI program, challenging the idea that students must master controlled texts first.
The author argues it is possible to praise DI while accepting that other approaches to accelerating reading also work, and that a fair account of the evidence should say so.
Her open questions concern whether DI programs leave room for students to analyse, interpret and build robust comprehension of rich text.
quotes: When a student doesn’t understand something, it’s probably not the student that’s the problem. It’s probably the teaching.
I would love to see more teachers incorporate some of this stuff into their own teaching (more likely). I would also love to see more curriculum companies take these ideas seriously (less likely).
While both groups made similar gains on oral reading fluency, the Read Like Us students made greater gains in oral reading accuracy, despite reading much more complicated and sophisticated texts.
This study also reminds us that there are other, viable approaches to accelerating literacy acquisition for striving readers. To be clear, this is a good thing.
I also hope that, over the next five episodes, Emily Hanford proceeds to complicate the story she’s telling.
How much opportunity do students have to grapple with meaning in DI programs? Where does student analysis and interpretation fit into DI?
